paras: The shooting of Louis Guilford took place at Tarboro, North Carolina, on October 23, 1882, when Guilford, a Black man under arrest, was shot and mortally wounded by men who pursued and recaptured him after he escaped. According to the dispatch, Guilford had cut the arresting constable with a razor and wounded two of his captors, and papers across the country ran the story as the act of a "fighting" or "murderous" Black man.
On the morning of Monday, October 23, Constable J. J. Durford of Tarboro arrested Guilford, described as "a negro" or "a colored man," for an assault whose details were not given.

On the way to jail, the dispatch said, Guilford drew a razor and cut Durford across the abdomen, and as the constable "sank to the ground to die" Guilford ran off. Several men pursued and captured him, and the fuller wire version said he "seriously wounded two of his captors" before he was "finally shot and mortally wounded." None of the reports named the men who pursued him or the one who fired, or said where in Tarboro the shooting happened.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of the shooters or confirmation that either Guilford or Durford died appears in the coverage, which ended with a Virginia weekly reprint on November 9.

The story reached the press as a single Tarboro telegram that western dailies printed on October 24 under headlines such as "A Fighting Negro" in the Eureka Daily Sentinel, "A Desperate Criminal" in the Cheyenne Daily Leader and "A Murderous Negro" in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. A condensed version in the Richmond Daily Dispatch on October 25, later copied by the Stephens City Star and the Clarke Courier, called Guilford "a colored man," called the constable's wound "mortal," and dropped the wounded captors. Every version told the story from the arresting side, and none questioned the shooting.

The versions differed in detail: the longer dispatch had Guilford wounding two captors before he was shot, the Daily Republican said "several of his pursuers," and the Richmond brief said he was shot before his capture. Durford's injury was a "terrible" wound in the dispatch but a "fatal" or "mortal" one in the condensed items, and the constable's name was also printed as "Derford" and "Dufford."

reader.title: Shooting of Louis Guilford
bases: Guilford, under arrest by a constable, was shot and mortally wounded by the men who pursued and recaptured him after he escaped, not taken from custody by a mob (A1, A3, A9).

The wire account has Guilford 'pursued by several men' and 'finally shot and mortally wounded' during a capture in which he wounded two captors (A3, A4); nothing in the coverage describes a killing after he was subdued or a mob acting outside the arrest, though no report says who fired or under what authority.
Every report descends from one Tarboro dispatch of October 23, in a longer wire form (A1, A3, A4) and a condensed brief (A9, A11, A15); no local or independent account was found.

accounts.label: Tarboro wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Guilford cut the constable on the way to jail, ran, was pursued by several men and captured, seriously wounded two captors, and was finally shot and mortally wounded.

accounts.label: Condensed brief
accounts.gist: Guilford slashed the constable, inflicting a mortal wound, ran off and was captured, 'but not before he was shot and fatally wounded'; no wounded captors mentioned.

framing.detail: Western dailies ran the dispatch under headlines casting Guilford as the aggressor: 'A Fighting Negro', 'A Desperate Criminal', 'A Murderous Negro'.
Virginia papers and the Daily Republican ran it as a one-paragraph item among other news, calling Guilford 'a colored man'.
